name: Health & Fitness
tagline: Move more, eat better and feel strong every day.
description: No gym or equipment needed. Learn simple ways to move, eat, drink water and sit better, one small habit at a time. This is general health education, not medical advice.

messages.welcome: You do not need to be fit to start, you start to become fit. We will build one small habit at a time, and your body will thank you for each one.
messages.comeback: Your body has not forgotten you. Open the next lesson, stand up for two minutes, and let that small win pull you back in.
messages.pass: Strong work. That idea is now part of how you take care of yourself.
messages.fail: Every rep counts, even the missed ones. Read the explanations, review the lesson and try again.
messages.finished: You can now move with purpose, fuel yourself well, stay hydrated, protect your posture, plan a balanced routine and keep it going through busy seasons. Pick one habit from this path and make it part of your week.

lessons.title: Why moving your body matters
lessons.content:
Your body is like a bicycle. If you ride it often, the chain stays smooth and the wheels spin easily. Leave it in the corner for months and it gets rusty and stiff. Moving your body works the same way. When you run, walk, jump or play, your heart, muscles and bones all get a little practice, and practice makes them stronger.

Here's why that matters. When you move every day, your heart pumps blood more easily, so you get tired less quickly on stairs or in a football match. Your muscles and bones get stronger, which is a big deal while you are still growing. Movement also makes your brain release chemicals that lift your mood, so you feel calmer before an exam and you fall asleep faster at night. Without enough movement, you feel sleepy in class, get grumpy more easily and lose your breath doing simple things.

So how much is enough? Health experts say kids and teens should get about 60 minutes of movement every day. That is one hour, but it does not have to be in one go. Ten minutes of cycling, 20 minutes of cricket after school, 10 minutes of walking to the shop and 20 minutes of skipping rope already make 60.

Here's the trick: count what you already do, then add a little. Moderate movement means your heart beats faster and you breathe harder, but you can still talk. A slow stroll to the fridge does not count much. A fast walk, running, dancing, swimming or playing badminton does. A few times a week, try something that makes you puff harder, like racing your friend or running up stairs.

Take Rafi, a class 6 student in Dhaka. He went to school by rickshaw, sat in class, went to tuition, then played games on his phone. When he counted, he moved only about 15 minutes a day. He started walking to tuition, which took 15 minutes each way, and played cricket in the lane for 30 minutes. That made an hour. After three weeks, he was not yawning in class anymore and he could bat longer without getting tired.

The common mistake is thinking only a "real workout" counts, so you wait for a gym or a perfect plan and do nothing. Walking, chores, playing and climbing stairs all count. Start with what you can do today.

Remember this: about 60 minutes of movement a day, in small pieces, keeps your body and mind working well.
key_points: Moving every day makes your heart, muscles and bones stronger.
Kids and teens should aim for about 60 minutes of movement a day.
Short pieces like 10 or 20 minutes add up to the full hour.
Movement also improves mood, focus and sleep.
lessons.tip: Pick one trip you usually take by rickshaw or car, like going to a nearby shop or tuition, and walk it instead.
lessons.task: Write down every time you moved today, like walking, playing, stairs or chores, and how many minutes each took. Add them up and see how close you are to 60.

quiz.q: How much movement a day do health experts suggest for kids and teens?
quiz.explain: The common guideline for kids and teens is about 60 minutes of movement every day.

quiz.q: Which of these best shows that the movement is moderate?
options: Your heart beats faster but you can still talk
quiz.explain: Moderate movement makes your heart beat faster and your breathing harder, but you can still talk.

quiz.q: How did Rafi reach about an hour of movement a day?
options: He did one 60-minute run every morning
He walked to tuition and played cricket in the lane
quiz.explain: Rafi added a 15-minute walk each way to tuition plus 30 minutes of cricket, which made an hour.

lessons.title: Walking: the easiest workout
lessons.content:
Walking is exercise you already know how to do. You do not need shoes from a big brand, a gym or any money. Think of it like the "starter level" of a game: easy to begin, but you can still level it up by walking faster and longer.

Why bother, if it is so easy? Because a brisk walk makes your heart and lungs work harder, and that is what trains them. Walking strengthens your leg muscles and bones, clears your head when you have been studying for hours, and helps you digest food after a big meal. If you skip it and sit all day instead, your legs get weak, your back gets stiff and you feel tired even though you did nothing.

The key is pace, not just steps. A slow stroll is nice but does not train much. A brisk walk does. To check, use the talk test. If you can sing a song easily, you are too slow. If you can talk in full sentences but not sing, that is perfect brisk walking. If you can only gasp out one or two words, slow down a bit.

Here's how to start. Walk 10 minutes at a brisk pace, three times this week. Next week, make it 15 minutes. Keep adding 5 minutes a week until you reach 20 to 30 minutes most days. Stand tall, look ahead instead of at your phone, and swing your arms. Wear comfortable shoes that hold your feet well, and carry water if it is hot. Walk in safe places like a park, the school field or a quiet lane, and watch out for traffic.

Meet Nusrat from Chattogram. She felt tired every afternoon and her mother said she spent too long on Facebook. Nusrat started walking with her mother in the evening around the neighbourhood. In the first week, they walked 10 minutes and chatted the whole way, which meant it was brisk but not too hard. By the fourth week, they were walking 25 minutes. Nusrat said her afternoons felt lighter, she slept better, and she had a nice time with her mother every day.

The common mistake is walking slowly while looking at the phone and thinking it is a workout. Strolling and scrolling barely raises your heart rate. Put the phone in your pocket and walk with purpose.

Remember: walk brisk enough that you can talk but not sing, and add 5 minutes a week.
key_points: Walking needs no gym or money and still trains your heart.
Use the talk test: you can talk, but you cannot sing.
Start with 10 minutes and add 5 minutes each week.
Stand tall, swing your arms and keep the phone away.
lessons.tip: Walk with a friend or family member and keep chatting. If you can talk but cannot sing, your pace is just right.
lessons.task: Go for a 10-minute brisk walk today. Halfway through, try singing a line of a song. If it is easy, walk faster.

quiz.q: According to the talk test, what does brisk walking feel like?
options: You can talk but not sing
You can only gasp one word
quiz.explain: Brisk walking means you can talk in sentences but not sing. Easy singing means you are too slow.

quiz.q: How does the lesson suggest you increase your walks?
options: Walk 2 hours on the first day
quiz.explain: Start with 10 minutes and add about 5 minutes each week until you reach 20 to 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Why did Nusrat's walk count as brisk in the first week?
options: She sang loudly the whole time
She ran as fast as she could
She chatted with her mother but was moving with purpose
She stopped every minute to check Facebook
quiz.explain: She could talk the whole way while walking with purpose, which matches brisk walking.

lessons.title: Warm up, cool down, stay safe
lessons.content:
A warm-up is like warming up a cold pan before you cook. If you drop an egg into a cold pan, it sticks and cooks badly. Your muscles are similar. Cold muscles are stiff. A few minutes of easy movement warms them up so they stretch and work smoothly. A cool-down is the opposite: you slow down gently at the end instead of stopping suddenly.

Why do this? When you jump straight into fast running or a hard game, your muscles and joints are not ready, so you are more likely to pull a muscle or twist an ankle. A warm-up raises your heart rate slowly, loosens your joints and gets your mind ready too. A cool-down lets your heart and breathing come back to normal calmly, so you are less likely to feel dizzy.

Here's a 5-minute warm-up. March on the spot for 1 minute, lifting your knees. Do 10 big arm circles forward and 10 backward. Swing each leg forward and back gently 10 times, holding a wall for balance. Do 10 hip circles each way. Finish with 1 minute of light jogging on the spot. Notice these are moving stretches. Long still stretches are better at the end, not at the start.

For the cool-down, spend 3 to 5 minutes walking slowly until your breathing settles. Then do gentle still stretches. Hold each one for about 20 to 30 seconds without bouncing: reach for your toes for the back of the legs, pull one foot behind you for the front of the thigh, and pull one arm across your chest for the shoulder. Stretching should feel like a gentle pull, never pain. And the safety rules: drink water, stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest pain and tell an adult, and do not exercise hard when you are sick with a fever.

Sabbir loved football. Every Friday he ran straight onto the field and started sprinting. Twice in one month, he felt a sharp pull in the back of his thigh and had to sit out. His PE teacher showed him the 5-minute warm-up. Sabbir started doing it with his friends before every match, and they made it a team ritual. For the rest of the season, he did not pull a muscle once, and he felt faster in the first ten minutes of the game.

The common mistake is doing long, still stretches on cold muscles at the start, or bouncing in a stretch. Warm up with moving exercises first, and save the still stretches for after.

Remember: 5 minutes of moving warm-up before, slow walk and gentle stretches after, and stop if anything hurts sharply.
key_points: A warm-up gets cold, stiff muscles ready and lowers injury risk.
Warm up with moving exercises like marching, arm circles and leg swings.
Cool down with slow walking, then hold gentle stretches for 20 to 30 seconds.
Stop and tell an adult if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest pain.
lessons.tip: Turn your warm-up into a habit by doing it to one favourite song. When the song ends, your 5-minute warm-up is done.
lessons.task: Do the 5-minute warm-up from this lesson right now: march, arm circles, leg swings, hip circles and light jogging. Then do the three cool-down stretches for 20 seconds each.

quiz.q: Which type of movement is best for a warm-up?
options: Long still stretches held for a minute
Moving exercises like arm circles and leg swings
quiz.explain: Warm-ups should use moving exercises that slowly raise your heart rate and loosen your joints.

quiz.q: How long should you hold a gentle stretch in a cool-down?
quiz.explain: Hold each cool-down stretch for about 20 to 30 seconds, as a gentle pull without bouncing or pain.

quiz.q: What changed for Sabbir after he started warming up?
options: He stopped pulling muscles and felt faster early in the game
He had to sit out every match
He only did still stretches before sprinting
quiz.explain: With a 5-minute warm-up before every match, Sabbir did not pull a muscle again that season.

lessons.title: Your first bodyweight moves
lessons.content:
Bodyweight exercises use your own body as the weight. Instead of lifting dumbbells, you lift yourself. Think of it like carrying your school bag up the stairs: the weight is already there, you just have to move it. Three simple moves are enough to start: the squat, the push-up and the plank.

Why do these? Strong muscles help you run faster, jump higher, carry heavy things like a bazar bag without hurting your back, and keep good posture while sitting in class. For kids and teens, bodyweight exercises done with good form are safe and help bones grow strong too. Without any strength work, simple things like climbing stairs or carrying a water bottle crate feel much harder than they should.

The squat: stand with feet about shoulder-width apart. Push your hips back like you are sitting on a chair, bend your knees and keep your chest up and heels on the floor. Go down as low as feels comfortable, then stand up. Put a chair behind you if you want a target. The push-up: hands on the floor a bit wider than your shoulders, body straight like a plank of wood from head to heels, lower your chest towards the floor, then push back up. Too hard? Do it with your knees on the floor, or with your hands on a table or wall.

The plank: rest on your forearms and toes, keep your body in a straight line, squeeze your tummy and do not let your hips sag or stick up. Start with 15 to 20 seconds. Here's a simple routine: 10 squats, 5 push-ups (any version) and a 15-second plank. Rest 1 minute and repeat 2 times. Do it 2 or 3 days a week, with a rest day in between. When it feels easy, add 2 more squats or push-ups, or 5 more seconds on the plank.

Tania, class 7, could not do a single floor push-up and felt embarrassed in PE class. She started doing wall push-ups at home, 3 rounds of 8, three times a week. After two weeks, she moved to the table. After a month, she did knee push-ups on the floor, and after two months, she managed 3 full push-ups. She also noticed carrying her heavy school bag no longer made her shoulders ache.

The common mistake is chasing big numbers with bad form, like letting the hips sag in a push-up or knees cave inward in a squat. Five good reps are better than twenty sloppy ones. Slow down and do it right.

Remember: squat, push-up, plank, with good form, 2 or 3 times a week, adding a little when it gets easy.
key_points: Bodyweight exercises use your own body as the weight, no equipment needed.
Start with squats, push-ups and planks, using easier versions if needed.
Try 10 squats, 5 push-ups and a 15-second plank, repeated 2 to 3 times.
Good form matters more than the number of reps.
lessons.tip: If a full push-up is too hard, use the wall, then a table, then your knees. Move to the next level only when you can do 3 rounds of 8 with good form.
lessons.task: Do one round right now: 10 squats, 5 push-ups (wall, table, knee or full) and a 15-second plank. Write down which push-up version you used.

quiz.q: In a good squat, what should you do?
options: Push your hips back and keep your heels on the floor
Lift your heels and lean far forward
quiz.explain: A good squat pushes the hips back like sitting on a chair, with chest up and heels on the floor.

quiz.q: If a full push-up is too hard, what does the lesson suggest?
options: Bounce your chest off the floor
Do them against a wall, a table or on your knees
Let your hips sag to make it easier
quiz.explain: Wall, table and knee push-ups are easier versions that build strength towards a full push-up.

quiz.q: How did Tania get to her first full push-ups?
options: She tried 50 floor push-ups on day one
She did nothing and waited to get stronger
She moved step by step from wall to table to knee push-ups
quiz.explain: Tania progressed from wall to table to knee push-ups over two months, then managed 3 full push-ups.

lessons.title: Build a balanced plate
lessons.content:
A balanced plate is a simple way to check your meal just by looking at it. Imagine your plate is a clock. From 12 to 6, half the plate, goes vegetables and some fruit. From 6 to 9, a quarter, goes protein like fish, egg, dal or chicken. From 9 to 12, the last quarter, goes rice, roti or another carb. No counting, no weighing, just a quick look.

Why does this matter? Your body needs different foods for different jobs. Carbs give quick energy, protein builds and repairs muscles, and vegetables and fruit bring vitamins, minerals and fibre that keep your stomach working and help you fight off illness. A plate that is mostly rice with a tiny bit of curry gives a burst of energy, then you feel sleepy and hungry again soon. A balanced plate keeps you full and focused for longer.

Here's how to build it with normal home food. Start by putting the vegetables on first: shak, lau, begun bhaji, a salad of cucumber and tomato, or mixed vegetable curry. Fill half the plate. Then add your protein: one piece of fish, one egg, a bowl of dal or a piece of chicken. Then add rice or roti in the last quarter. If you usually take three scoops of rice, try two, and add more vegetables in that space.

You do not need a perfect plate at every meal. Aim to get close at lunch and dinner. If one meal is light on vegetables, add some at the next one, or have a fruit like a guava, banana or a slice of papaya as a snack. And drink water with your meal instead of soft drinks.

Sabbir, class 6, loved a big mountain of rice with a little chicken curry. He always felt sleepy in afternoon tuition. His mother suggested the clock trick. Sabbir started taking two scoops of rice instead of three, added a big spoon of mixed vegetables and kept his piece of chicken. At first it felt strange, but within a week he noticed he was not dozing off in tuition anymore, and he did not need chips at 5 pm.

The common mistake is thinking a balanced plate means you must stop eating rice. Rice is fine. The point is the amount: a quarter of the plate, with vegetables taking the biggest space.

Remember: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein, a quarter rice or roti.
key_points: Think of your plate as a clock: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter carbs.
Carbs give energy, protein builds muscle, vegetables bring vitamins and fibre.
Put vegetables on your plate first so they take the biggest space.
You do not have to quit rice, just keep it to about a quarter.
lessons.tip: Serve the vegetables onto your plate first, before the rice. Whatever goes on first usually takes the most space.
lessons.task: At your next meal, look at your plate before eating. Guess how much is vegetables, protein and rice. If vegetables are less than half, add one more spoonful.

quiz.q: On a balanced plate, how much should be vegetables and fruit?
quiz.explain: The balanced plate puts vegetables and fruit on about half, with protein and carbs sharing the other half.

quiz.q: Which of these is a protein food from the lesson?
quiz.explain: Dal, fish, eggs and chicken are protein foods. Rice and roti are carbs, and lau shak is a vegetable.

quiz.q: What did Sabbir change on his plate?
options: He took more rice and less chicken
He took less rice and added vegetables
He drank soft drinks with his meal
quiz.explain: Sabbir went from three scoops of rice to two, added vegetables and kept his chicken.

lessons.title: Protein, carbs and fats made simple
lessons.content:
Most of your food is made of three big building blocks: protein, carbohydrates (carbs) and fats. Imagine your body is a house being built. Protein is the bricks that build walls and fix cracks. Carbs are the electricity that keeps the lights on and the machines running. Fats are like the insulation and wiring that protect things and help the house work properly. You need all three.

Why should you know this? Because if you skip one, something goes wrong. Too little protein and your muscles struggle to grow and repair, and you feel hungry quickly. Too few carbs and you feel weak and foggy, especially in sport or long exams. Too little healthy fat and your body cannot use some vitamins well. But too much sugar or fried oily food leaves you tired and can harm your heart over many years.

Here's where to find each one. Protein: fish, eggs, chicken, dal, chickpeas (chola), milk, yogurt (doi) and nuts. Carbs: rice, roti, bread, potatoes, oats, fruit and also sugar. Fats: cooking oil, ghee, butter, nuts, peanuts, egg yolk and fish like hilsa. The trick is to choose the better kind of each. For carbs, choose ones that fill you up longer, like brown or red rice, atta roti, oats, fruit and vegetables, instead of sweets, soft drinks and white bread all the time.

For fats, the better kind comes from nuts, seeds, fish and normal amounts of cooking oil. Cut down on deep-fried food like puri, singara and fried chicken, which soak up lots of oil. A simple rule: try to have one protein food at every meal, carbs that are mostly not sugary, and fried snacks only a few times a week.

Tania, class 7, ate paratha with tea for breakfast and was starving by 10 am. She often bought a packet of chips at school. Her elder sister told her to add protein. Tania started eating a boiled egg with her roti, or a bowl of doi with some chira. Now she stays full until lunch, stopped buying chips, and saves her tiffin money for something else.

The common mistake is thinking all fat or all carbs are bad and trying to cut them out completely. Your body needs both. The problem is too much sugar and too much deep-fried food, not rice or a little oil.

Remember: protein builds, carbs power, fats protect, so eat all three and pick the less sugary, less fried kinds.
key_points: Protein builds and repairs, carbs give energy, fats protect and help use vitamins.
Have one protein food, like egg, fish or dal, at every meal.
Pick carbs like atta roti, oats and fruit more often than sweets and soft drinks.
Keep deep-fried snacks to a few times a week.
lessons.tip: Add one protein food to your breakfast, like a boiled egg, a bowl of doi or some chola. It keeps you full until lunch.
lessons.task: Write down what you ate yesterday. Next to each food, write P for protein, C for carbs or F for fats. Find one meal that had no protein.

quiz.q: In the house example, what is protein like?
options: The bricks that build and fix walls
quiz.explain: Protein is like bricks: it builds and repairs muscles and other parts of the body.

quiz.q: Which is a better carb choice for lasting energy?
quiz.explain: Atta roti, oats, fruit and vegetables keep you full longer than sugary foods and drinks.

quiz.q: What helped Tania stay full until lunch?
options: Adding a protein food like an egg or doi to breakfast
quiz.explain: Adding protein, like a boiled egg or doi, made her breakfast keep her full for longer.

lessons.title: Water and hydration
lessons.content:
More than half of your body is water. Think of water as the delivery service of your body. It carries food and oxygen to every part, takes away waste, keeps your joints smooth and cools you down by sweating. Being hydrated simply means you have enough water in your body for all these jobs.

Why does it matter so much? When you do not drink enough, even a little, you can get a headache, feel tired, find it hard to concentrate and feel cranky. Many people think they are hungry or bored when they are actually thirsty. In Bangladesh's hot, humid weather, you sweat a lot, especially after playing outside, so you lose water fast. When you drink enough, you think more clearly, play longer and feel fresher.

How much should you drink? There is no single perfect number, because it depends on the weather, your size and how active you are. A simple guide for kids is about 6 to 8 glasses a day, and more on hot days or when you play sport. Food like fruit, dal and curry also gives some water. The easiest check is your pee: pale yellow, like lemon juice, means you are doing well. Dark yellow means drink more.

Here's how to make it easy. Drink one glass of water when you wake up. Carry a water bottle to school and try to finish it before you come home. Drink a glass with each meal. Before, during and after playing, take a few sips every 15 to 20 minutes. Choose plain water most of the time. Soft drinks and packaged juices have lots of sugar, so keep them for special days. And drink safe water: boiled or filtered, especially outside the home.

Rafi often got headaches during afternoon tuition. He thought it was the maths. His mother noticed he came home with his water bottle still full. Rafi made a rule: finish half the bottle before tiffin and the other half before school ends. After a week, his afternoon headaches mostly went away, and his pee was pale instead of dark yellow.

The common mistake is waiting until you feel very thirsty. By the time you are really thirsty, your body is already a bit low on water. Sip regularly through the day instead of gulping a lot at once.

Remember: about 6 to 8 glasses a day, more when it is hot, and check that your pee is pale yellow.
key_points: Water carries nutrients, removes waste and cools your body.
Even a little dehydration can cause headaches, tiredness and poor focus.
Aim for about 6 to 8 glasses a day, and more on hot or active days.
Pale yellow pee means you are drinking enough.
lessons.tip: Split your school water bottle into two goals: half before tiffin, the other half before school ends.
lessons.task: Fill a glass of water and drink it now. Then decide on three moments tomorrow when you will drink a glass, like after waking up, at lunch and after playing.

quiz.q: What is an easy sign that you are drinking enough water?
quiz.explain: Pale yellow pee usually means you are well hydrated. Dark yellow means you should drink more.

quiz.q: What should you do when playing sport on a hot day?
options: Drink a soft drink instead of water
Avoid drinking so you do not get a stomach ache
Take a few sips every 15 to 20 minutes
quiz.explain: Sipping water before, during and after sport helps replace the water you lose by sweating.

quiz.q: What rule did Rafi make to drink more water?
options: Finish half his bottle before tiffin and half before school ends
Drink only when he gets a headache
quiz.explain: Rafi split his bottle into two goals during the school day, and his afternoon headaches mostly went away.

lessons.title: Smarter snacks and reading labels
lessons.content:
A snack is a small bite between meals. A good snack is like a bridge that carries you from lunch to dinner without falling into "I'm starving" mode. A food label is the small table and list printed on a packet that tells you what is really inside. Reading it is like checking the ingredients of a recipe before you cook.

Why does this matter? Many easy snacks, like chips, instant noodles, packaged cakes and sugary biscuits, are full of salt, sugar or oil but keep you full for only a short time. You eat them, feel good for 20 minutes, then feel hungry and tired again. Eaten every day, these add up to a lot of extra sugar and salt, which is not good for your teeth, your weight or your heart over the years. A smarter snack gives steady energy and actually helps your body.

Here's how to pick a smarter snack. Choose foods that are close to their natural form: fruit like banana, guava, apple or seasonal fruit, a handful of peanuts or chola, a boiled egg, doi, muri with some peanuts, or a roti with a little vegetable. Try to include some protein or fibre, because these keep you full longer than sugar alone.

When you do buy something in a packet, read the label in three steps. First, look at the serving size: a packet may say "per 25 g" but the whole packet may be 75 g, so eating it all means three times the numbers. Second, check the sugar. Every 4 grams of sugar is about 1 teaspoon. A drink with 32 g of sugar has about 8 teaspoons! Third, read the ingredients list. Ingredients are listed from most to least, so if sugar or oil is first or second, that food is mostly sugar or oil.

Nusrat bought a "healthy" fruit juice packet every day at school. One day, she read the label: 250 ml, 28 g of sugar. She divided by 4 and got 7 teaspoons of sugar. She was shocked. She switched to a banana or a guava from home plus her water bottle, and kept the juice for once a week. She saved money and stopped feeling sleepy in the last class.

The common mistake is trusting the front of the packet. Words like "natural", "real fruit" or "healthy" are just advertising. The truth is on the back, in the numbers and ingredients list.

Remember: choose snacks close to nature, and on packets, check serving size, sugar (4 g is 1 teaspoon) and the first ingredients.
key_points: Good snacks give steady energy, like fruit, peanuts, chola, eggs or doi.
On a label, check the serving size first, because a packet can have several servings.
Every 4 grams of sugar is about 1 teaspoon.
Ingredients are listed from most to least, so watch what comes first.
lessons.tip: Divide the grams of sugar on any drink label by 4. That is how many teaspoons of sugar you would be drinking.
lessons.task: Find one packaged food or drink at home. Read its label and work out the teaspoons of sugar in the whole packet. Write it on a small paper and stick it on the packet.

quiz.q: A drink has 32 g of sugar. About how many teaspoons is that?
quiz.explain: Every 4 g of sugar is about 1 teaspoon, so 32 g divided by 4 is about 8 teaspoons.

quiz.q: Why should you check the ingredients list order?
options: The front of the packet is always more accurate
Ingredients are listed from most to least
quiz.explain: The first ingredients make up most of the food. If sugar or oil is near the top, the food is mostly that.

quiz.q: What did Nusrat discover from her juice label?
options: It had about 7 teaspoons of sugar
It had no sugar at all
It was cheaper than a banana
quiz.explain: Her 250 ml juice had 28 g of sugar, and 28 divided by 4 is 7 teaspoons.

lessons.title: Posture basics
lessons.content:
Posture is how you hold your body when you sit, stand or walk. Good posture means your body is stacked like a neat pile of books: your ears above your shoulders, your shoulders above your hips. Bad posture is when the pile leans, like when your head pokes forward towards your phone and your back curves into a C.

Why care? Your head is heavy, about as heavy as a big watermelon. When it sits right on top of your spine, your bones carry it easily. When it leans forward to look at a phone, your neck and upper back muscles have to hold it up all the time, like holding a heavy bag with your arms stretched out. That is why many students get a sore neck, stiff shoulders or back pain after hours of study or phone use. Good posture also helps you breathe more deeply and look more confident.

Here's how to sit well. Sit back in the chair so your lower back touches the backrest. Keep both feet flat on the floor; if your feet do not reach, put a box or a few thick books under them. Let your shoulders relax down, not up near your ears. Keep your head over your shoulders, with your chin slightly tucked, as if a string is gently pulling the top of your head up.

To stand well, put your weight evenly on both feet, keep your knees soft, not locked, and let your arms hang loosely. For phones, bring the phone up closer to eye level instead of bending your neck down to it. And here's the big secret: no single posture is perfect for hours. The best posture is your next posture, so change position often.

Sabbir spent two hours every evening playing games on his phone, head bent down on his bed. He started getting neck pain. His elder brother told him to try the "string trick" and to hold the phone higher, resting his elbows on a pillow. He also sat at the table for homework instead of lying on the bed. In two weeks, the neck pain was almost gone, and he found it easier to focus on homework too.

The common mistake is trying to sit stiff and straight like a soldier for hours. That gets tiring quickly and you slump again. Good posture should feel relaxed and tall, and you should move often.

Remember: ears over shoulders, shoulders over hips, feet flat, and change position often.
key_points: Good posture stacks your ears over your shoulders and shoulders over your hips.
A forward head makes your neck and back muscles work hard all day.
Sit back in the chair with feet flat, shoulders relaxed and head over shoulders.
No position is perfect for hours, so change position often.
lessons.tip: Hold your phone up near eye level, resting your elbows on a table or pillow, instead of bending your neck down.
lessons.task: Stand with your back against a wall for one minute. Try to touch the wall with your heels, bottom, shoulders and the back of your head. Notice how that tall position feels, then sit down and copy it.

quiz.q: What does good posture look like?
options: Ears over shoulders and shoulders over hips
Shoulders raised up near the ears
Back curved into a C shape
quiz.explain: Good posture stacks your body: ears above shoulders and shoulders above hips.

quiz.q: If your feet do not reach the floor when sitting, what should you do?
options: Sit on the edge of the chair
Put a box or thick books under them
quiz.explain: A box or thick books under your feet lets them rest flat, which supports better sitting posture.

quiz.q: What helped Sabbir's neck pain?
options: Lying flat on the bed with the phone on his chest
Holding the phone higher and doing homework at a table
quiz.explain: Sabbir raised his phone, rested his elbows and moved homework to the table, and his neck pain eased.

lessons.title: Set up your study desk
lessons.content:
Setting up your desk means arranging your table, chair, books and screen so they fit your body, instead of twisting your body to fit them. Think of it like adjusting the seat and mirrors before riding a bicycle. A few small changes, and the whole ride becomes easier.

Why does it matter? You probably spend many hours a week doing homework, online classes or reading. If your screen is too low, you bend your neck. If the chair is too low, you lift your shoulders. If the light is poor, you squint and get headaches. These small strains add up into neck pain, sore eyes and tired wrists. A good setup lets you study longer with less pain and better focus, and it costs almost nothing.

Here's how to set up, from the bottom up. Feet: flat on the floor or on a box or stack of books. Chair: sit back so your lower back is supported; roll up a small towel and put it behind your lower back if the chair is flat. Table height: when your arms hang down and your elbows bend at about a right angle, your forearms should rest on the table without lifting your shoulders. If the table is too high, sit on a cushion.

Screen: the top of the screen should be at or slightly below your eyes, about an arm's length away. For a laptop, put it on a stack of books and, if you have one, use a separate keyboard. Books: prop them up on a book stand or a few books so you do not hunch over them. Light: sit with a window or lamp beside you, not behind the screen and not behind you causing glare. And look away often: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. This is called the 20-20-20 rule, and it rests your eyes.

Tania did her online classes on a laptop on her bed, looking down for hours. By evening, her eyes burned and her neck ached. Her father helped her move to the dining table. They put the laptop on three thick dictionaries, she used an old keyboard, and she sat with the window beside her. She set a phone timer for the 20-20-20 rule. Within a week, her eye strain and neck pain were much better.

The common mistake is thinking you need an expensive chair or desk. Books, cushions, towels and boxes fix most problems for free. What matters is the position, not the price.

Remember: feet flat, back supported, elbows at a right angle, screen top at eye level, and 20-20-20 for your eyes.
key_points: Arrange your desk to fit your body instead of bending your body to fit it.
Keep feet flat, back supported and elbows bent at about a right angle.
Put the top of the screen at or just below eye level, about an arm's length away.
Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
lessons.tip: Put your laptop on a stack of thick books so the top of the screen reaches your eye level.
lessons.task: Sit at your study place now. Check four things: feet flat, back supported, elbows at a right angle, and screen or book at eye level. Fix one thing using a book, cushion or towel.

quiz.q: Where should the top of your screen be?
options: At or slightly below eye level
quiz.explain: The top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level so your neck stays straight.

quiz.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
options: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
quiz.explain: Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds to rest your eyes.

quiz.q: How did Tania raise her laptop?
options: She put it on three thick dictionaries
She kept it on her bed
She held it on her knees
quiz.explain: Tania used three thick dictionaries to raise the laptop, which cost nothing and fixed her neck position.

lessons.title: Break up long sitting
lessons.content:
Breaking up sitting means standing up and moving for a minute or two every so often, instead of sitting for hours without a pause. Think of your body like a pond. Moving water stays fresh. Still water gets stale. When you sit still for too long, your body gets "stale" too.

Why does it matter? When you sit for a long time, your leg muscles hardly work, your blood moves more slowly and your body becomes stiff. You start to feel sleepy and your focus drops, so you read the same line three times. Over many years, lots of long, unbroken sitting is linked to weaker muscles, back pain and health problems like heart disease and diabetes. Short movement breaks wake your body and brain back up, and you often study better after one.

Here's the method. Every 30 minutes of sitting, stand up and move for 1 to 2 minutes. That is it. You can walk to the kitchen and drink water, do 10 squats, stretch your arms up high, march on the spot, or walk around the room while you think about what you just read. Use a timer on your phone or watch, or a simple rule like "every time I finish a chapter section, I stand up".

Add movement to things you already do. Stand up when you take a phone call. Walk to a classmate's house instead of messaging. During TV, stand up at every ad break. During online classes, stand and stretch between classes. At school, use tiffin break to walk around instead of sitting at your desk the whole time.

Rafi had a big exam coming and studied for three hours at a stretch every evening. By the second hour, he was yawning and forgetting what he read. His tuition teacher told him to stand up every 30 minutes. Rafi set a phone timer. When it rang, he filled his water glass, did 10 squats, and came back. He felt more awake, and he found that he remembered more because his brain had small pauses to settle the information.

The common mistake is thinking that one workout makes up for sitting all day. Even if you play football for an hour, sitting for six hours straight afterwards still makes your body stiff and sleepy. You need both: exercise and regular breaks.

Remember: every 30 minutes, stand up and move for 1 to 2 minutes.
key_points: Long, unbroken sitting makes you stiff, sleepy and less focused.
Every 30 minutes, stand up and move for 1 to 2 minutes.
Link movement to habits like phone calls, ad breaks and finishing a section.
One workout does not cancel out sitting for hours, so take breaks too.
lessons.tip: Set a 30-minute timer when you start studying. When it rings, drink water and do 10 squats before you reset it.
lessons.task: The next time you sit to study or watch something, set a 30-minute timer. When it rings, stand up and do 1 minute of movement: march, stretch or do 10 squats.

quiz.q: How often does the lesson suggest you stand up and move?
quiz.explain: The lesson suggests standing up and moving for 1 to 2 minutes every 30 minutes of sitting.

quiz.q: What happened to Rafi's studying after he started taking breaks?
options: He felt more awake and remembered more
He forgot more of what he read
quiz.explain: Short movement breaks helped Rafi stay awake and remember more of what he studied.

quiz.q: Does one hour of football cancel out sitting for six hours straight?
options: No, you still need regular breaks from sitting
quiz.explain: Exercise is great, but you still need to break up long periods of sitting during the day.

lessons.title: Stretches for desk life
lessons.content:
A stretch is when you gently lengthen a muscle and hold it there for a little while. Imagine a rubber band that has been folded in a drawer for days. Pull it gently a few times and it becomes loose and springy again. Muscles that stay in one position for hours, like when you sit and study, get tight in the same way.

Why stretch? Hours at a desk tighten your neck, shoulders, chest, back, hips and wrists. Tight muscles pull your body out of good posture, cause stiffness and can make your neck or back ache. Gentle stretches through the day loosen them, make it easier to sit tall and help you feel fresh. You do not need a mat or special clothes; most of these can be done in your chair.

Here's a 3-minute desk stretch routine. Neck: slowly tilt your right ear towards your right shoulder and hold for 15 to 20 seconds, then the left. Shoulder rolls: lift your shoulders up to your ears, roll them back and down, 10 times. Chest opener: clasp your hands behind your back, gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and lift your chest, hold 15 to 20 seconds. This undoes the hunched-forward position.

Seated twist: sit tall, put your right hand on the back of your chair and gently turn your upper body to the right, hold 15 seconds, then the left. Wrist stretch: hold one arm out, palm up, and use the other hand to gently pull the fingers down, hold 15 seconds, then switch. Hip and leg: stand up, hold the chair and pull one foot behind you towards your bottom, hold 15 to 20 seconds each side. Breathe slowly the whole time. Each stretch should feel like a gentle pull, never a sharp pain. Do this routine two or three times a day, for example after each long study session.

Nusrat spent the evening typing assignments on her mother's laptop and writing notes. Her shoulders felt like stones by bedtime. She made a sticky note with six words: "neck, roll, chest, twist, wrist, leg". She stuck it on her table. After every hour, she did the routine. In a week, her shoulders felt loose at night, and she even taught it to her younger brother, who copied her during his homework.

The common mistake is bouncing or pushing a stretch until it hurts, thinking more pain means more benefit. Bouncing can strain the muscle. Go to a gentle pull, hold still and breathe.

Remember: neck, shoulders, chest, twist, wrists and legs, held gently for 15 to 20 seconds, a few times a day.
key_points: Sitting for hours tightens the neck, shoulders, chest, back, hips and wrists.
Hold each stretch for about 15 to 20 seconds, gently, without bouncing.
A chest opener helps undo the hunched-forward desk position.
Do a short stretch routine two or three times a day.
lessons.tip: Write the six stretch words, neck, roll, chest, twist, wrist, leg, on a sticky note and put it on your study table.
lessons.task: Do the full 3-minute routine from this lesson now: neck tilt, shoulder rolls, chest opener, seated twist, wrist stretch and standing leg stretch.

quiz.q: How long should you hold each desk stretch?
quiz.explain: Each stretch should be held gently for about 15 to 20 seconds.

quiz.q: Which stretch helps undo a hunched-forward position?
quiz.explain: Clasping your hands behind you and lifting your chest opens up the front of your body.

quiz.q: What did Nusrat use to remember her routine?
options: A sticky note with six stretch words
quiz.explain: Nusrat wrote six short words on a sticky note and kept it on her table as a reminder.

lessons.title: The four parts of a complete routine
lessons.content:
A complete fitness routine has four parts: cardio, strength, flexibility and balance. Think of it like a cricket team. You need batters, bowlers, a wicketkeeper and fielders. A team of only bowlers would lose. Your body is the same: doing only one kind of exercise leaves gaps.

Here's what each part does and why you need it. Cardio is anything that makes your heart beat faster for a while, like running, cycling, skipping, swimming or a fast game of football. It trains your heart and lungs so you do not get out of breath easily. Strength work, like squats, push-ups and planks, builds muscles and bones so you can lift, push and carry things. Flexibility, like stretching, keeps your joints moving freely so you do not feel stiff. Balance, like standing on one leg, helps you stay steady and avoid falls when you run, turn or jump.

If you only do cardio, you may run well but struggle to carry heavy things. If you only do strength, you may be strong but stiff and get tired quickly in a match. A mix makes you good at everything you do in daily life and sport.

Here's how much of each to aim for. Cardio: most days, as part of your 60 minutes of daily activity. Strength: 2 or 3 days a week, with a rest day in between for the same muscles. Flexibility: a few minutes after every workout, or the desk stretches during the day. Balance: a minute or two a few times a week. For example, stand on one leg for 30 seconds while brushing your teeth, then switch. When it gets easy, try it with your eyes closed, near a wall for safety.

Sabbir was a fast runner and ran every day, but in football matches he kept getting knocked over and his hamstrings felt tight. His coach noticed he did only running. Sabbir added squats and push-ups on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, stretched for 5 minutes after every run, and practised standing on one leg while brushing his teeth. After a month, he was harder to push off the ball, his legs felt looser, and he stopped tripping when he turned quickly.

The common mistake is sticking only to the exercise you already like and are good at. Most people love one type and skip the rest. Keep your favourite, but add a little of the other three.

Remember: cardio for the heart, strength for muscles and bones, flexibility for loose joints, balance for steadiness, and include all four each week.
key_points: A complete routine has cardio, strength, flexibility and balance.
Cardio trains heart and lungs; strength builds muscles and bones.
Do strength 2 or 3 days a week and stretch after workouts.
Practise balance, like standing on one leg while brushing your teeth.
lessons.tip: Practise balance while brushing your teeth: stand on one leg for 30 seconds, then switch legs.
lessons.task: Write the four parts, cardio, strength, flexibility and balance, on a paper. Next to each, write one activity you did this week. Circle the part with nothing next to it and pick one activity to try tomorrow.

quiz.q: Which part of a routine trains your heart and lungs?
quiz.explain: Cardio, like running, cycling and skipping, trains your heart and lungs.

quiz.q: How often should you do strength exercises?
options: 2 or 3 days a week with rest days between
quiz.explain: Strength work 2 or 3 days a week, with rest days between, gives muscles time to recover.

quiz.q: What was missing from Sabbir's routine at first?
quiz.explain: Sabbir only ran. He added strength, stretching and balance, which made him steadier and stronger in matches.

lessons.title: Plan your weekly workout
lessons.content:
A weekly workout plan is a simple timetable that says what exercise you will do on which day and at what time. It is just like your school class routine: you know maths is on Sunday at 10, so you are ready for it. Without a routine, exercise turns into "I'll do it when I have time", and busy days never seem to have time.

Why plan? When exercise has a fixed slot, you do not have to decide every day, and deciding is where most people give up. A plan also helps you include all four parts, cardio, strength, flexibility and balance, and give your muscles rest days. Without a plan, you may do too much one week, feel sore, then do nothing the next.

Here's how to make a plan in four steps. Step 1: look at your real week, school, tuition, coaching, homework, family time and prayers, and find gaps of 20 to 30 minutes. Step 2: pick 4 or 5 of those gaps and give each one a job. Step 3: spread strength days apart, like Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, so your muscles rest in between. Step 4: write it down and put it where you will see it, like the wall next to your study table or your phone's lock screen.

Here's an example. Saturday: 30 minutes cycling or playing outside. Sunday: 20 minutes strength (squats, push-ups, plank) plus stretches. Monday: 25 minutes brisk walk. Tuesday: strength again. Wednesday: rest or light walk. Thursday: strength plus balance practice. Friday: football or cricket with friends. Keep a backup plan too: if it rains, do 15 minutes of skipping or a home bodyweight circuit instead. Start small. A plan of 3 days you actually do is better than a plan of 7 days you quit.

Tania kept saying she would exercise "from tomorrow". She sat with her class routine and noticed she was free from 5:00 to 5:30 pm on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, and on Saturday morning. She wrote "5 pm: squats + push-ups + plank" on those days and "Saturday: walk with Nanu in the park". She stuck it next to her class routine. For the first time, she exercised four days a week for a whole month, because she never had to wonder when.

The common mistake is making an overly ambitious plan, like an hour every single day, then quitting after a week. Start with what fits your real life, then add more later.

Remember: find real gaps, give each one a job, spread strength days apart, write it down, and keep a rainy-day backup.
key_points: A weekly plan gives exercise a fixed day and time, like a class routine.
Find real 20 to 30 minute gaps in your week and give each one a job.
Spread strength days apart so muscles get rest in between.
Start small and keep a rainy-day backup plan.
lessons.tip: Write your workout plan right next to your class routine, so you see both together every day.
lessons.task: Look at your schedule for next week and find three gaps of 20 minutes or more. Write down what exercise you will do in each one, including the day and time.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a weekly plan?
options: Look at your real week and find free gaps
quiz.explain: Start by looking at your real schedule and finding 20 to 30 minute gaps you can use.

quiz.q: Why should strength days be spread apart?
options: So you have more homework time
So muscles get time to rest and recover
Because strength only works on weekends
quiz.explain: Spreading strength days apart gives your muscles rest days to recover and grow stronger.

quiz.q: What made Tania finally stick to exercise?
options: She waited for a perfect day
She planned an hour every day
She wrote fixed days and times next to her class routine
quiz.explain: Tania used real free slots and wrote them down next to her class routine, so she never had to decide when.

lessons.title: Progress without injury
lessons.content:
Progress means slowly making your workouts a little harder so your body keeps getting stronger. Your body is like a student. If you give it the same easy class 1 maths every day, it stops learning. If you suddenly give it university maths, it gets confused and gives up. The trick is to give it the next class up, one small step at a time.

Why does this matter? Once a workout feels easy, your body has already adapted to it, so doing the same thing forever stops making you fitter. But jumping up too fast is how people get hurt. Muscles get stronger fairly quickly, while tendons, joints and bones take longer to catch up. Doing too much too soon can lead to strains, sore joints and having to stop for weeks, which wipes out your progress.

Here's the safe method. Change only one thing at a time: either do a few more reps, or add a little more time, or try a slightly harder version, but not all three together. A simple rule: increase by about 10 percent or less per week. If you walk 20 minutes now, next week walk 22. If you do 10 squats, next week try 11 or 12. When you can do 3 rounds of a move easily with good form, it is time to move up.

Listen to your body. Normal muscle soreness feels like a dull ache a day or two after a new workout, and it fades in a few days. That is fine. Sharp pain, pain in a joint, pain that makes you limp, swelling, or pain that gets worse while you exercise is a warning sign. Stop, rest, and tell a parent or teacher; if it does not get better, see a doctor. Also, sleep well and keep at least one or two rest days a week. Your body gets stronger while resting, not only while training.

Rafi saw a video of a boy doing 100 push-ups a day and copied it the very next day. He could not lift his arms properly for three days and his wrist hurt. He took a week off, then started again properly: 3 rounds of 6 knee push-ups, adding 1 rep to each round every week. After two months, he was doing 3 rounds of 8 full push-ups, with no pain at all.

The common mistake is "no pain, no gain", pushing through sharp pain to look tough. That turns a small problem into a big injury. Gentle soreness is okay; sharp pain means stop.

Remember: add a little at a time, change one thing at a time, rest well, and stop if you feel sharp pain.
key_points: To keep improving, make workouts a little harder over time.
Change one thing at a time and increase by about 10 percent or less per week.
Dull soreness that fades in a few days is normal; sharp or joint pain means stop.
Rest days and good sleep are when your body gets stronger.
lessons.tip: When you can do 3 rounds of a move easily with good form, add just 1 rep to each round next week.
lessons.task: Pick one exercise you do, like walking or squats. Write down what you do now, then write next week's target, adding no more than 10 percent.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to increase your training?
options: Change one thing at a time, by about 10 percent or less per week
Add reps, time and difficulty all at once
Copy the hardest video you can find
quiz.explain: Changing one thing at a time, by about 10 percent or less per week, lets your whole body adapt safely.

quiz.q: Which of these is a warning sign to stop exercising?
options: A sharp pain in a joint
quiz.explain: Sharp pain, joint pain, swelling or pain that makes you limp means stop and rest, and tell an adult.

quiz.q: How did Rafi build up push-ups safely the second time?
options: He started with knee push-ups and added 1 rep per round each week
He trained through his wrist pain
quiz.explain: Rafi started with 3 rounds of 6 knee push-ups and added 1 rep each week, reaching full push-ups without pain.

lessons.title: Track your progress
lessons.content:
Tracking means writing down what you do, like how many squats you did or how long you walked, so you can look back later and see how far you have come. It is like the height marks some families draw on a door frame for their kids. Day to day you cannot see yourself grow, but when you look at the marks from last year, the difference is obvious.

Why track? Progress in fitness is slow, so without records it is easy to feel like nothing is changing and give up. When you can see that you went from 5 push-ups to 12, or from a 10-minute walk to 25 minutes, you feel proud and want to keep going. Tracking also shows you what is working and what is not, and warns you if you are doing too much.

Here's what to track. Skip the bathroom scale as your main measure; your weight goes up and down every day with water and food, and for growing kids it naturally goes up as you get taller. Instead, track things you can do: number of push-ups or squats in one go, how long you can hold a plank, how many minutes you walked or played, and how many days you exercised this week. Also track how you feel: energy, sleep and mood on a 1 to 5 scale.

Here's how to do it simply. Use a small notebook, a notes app or a calendar on your wall. After each workout, write one line, for example: "Sun: 12 squats x 3, 6 knee push-ups x 3, plank 25 sec, energy 4". On the calendar, put a tick on every day you moved for at least 30 minutes, and try not to break the chain of ticks. Once a month, test yourself on the same three things, like max push-ups, plank time and a 1 km walk time, and compare with last month.

Nusrat felt like she was not getting any fitter, even after a month of workouts. Her cousin told her to look at her notebook. On day 1 she had written "plank 15 sec, 4 knee push-ups". On day 30, it said "plank 45 sec, 10 knee push-ups". She had tripled her plank! Seeing that on paper made her so happy she showed her friends, and two of them started tracking too.

The common mistake is tracking too much or only tracking body weight. Writing ten numbers every day gets boring and you stop. Weight alone can go up even when you are getting stronger. Track a few simple things that show what your body can do.

Remember: write one line after each workout, tick the calendar, and test the same three things once a month.
key_points: Tracking lets you see slow progress that you would otherwise miss.
Track what you can do, like reps, plank time and active minutes, not only weight.
Write one short line after each workout and tick a calendar.
Test the same three things once a month and compare.
lessons.tip: Hang a paper calendar near your bed and tick every day you move for 30 minutes. Try not to break the chain.
lessons.task: Test yourself now: count how many squats you can do with good form in one go and time your plank. Write both numbers with today's date, to compare in a month.

quiz.q: Why is the bathroom scale not the best main measure?
options: Weight goes up and down daily, and growing kids naturally gain
It is better to track nothing
quiz.explain: Weight changes every day with water and food, and kids naturally gain as they grow, so it does not show fitness well.

quiz.q: What is a good thing to track?
options: How many push-ups you can do in one go
Only the price of your shoes
quiz.explain: Tracking what your body can do, like push-ups, plank time and active minutes, shows real progress.

quiz.q: What did Nusrat discover in her notebook?
options: She had lost all her strength
She had forgotten to write anything
Her plank had gone from 15 to 45 seconds
quiz.explain: Her notes showed her plank went from 15 to 45 seconds in 30 days, which she would not have noticed without tracking.

lessons.title: Eat well on a small budget and a busy day
lessons.content:
Eating well on a budget means getting healthy food without spending a lot of money or time. Think of it like packing your school bag the night before. Five minutes of planning saves you from rushing and forgetting things in the morning. Food works the same way: a little planning beats grabbing whatever is nearest.

Why does it matter? When people are busy, tired or short of money, they often buy the quickest thing: chips, instant noodles, fried snacks from the roadside or a burger. These cost more than you think over a week and leave you hungry again soon. With a bit of planning, you can eat better and actually spend less. For example, a packet of chips and a soft drink every day can cost around 50 to 60 taka, while a banana and a boiled egg from home cost much less and keep you full longer.

Here's how. First, know the cheap healthy heroes. Dal, eggs, chola, seasonal vegetables, small fish, bananas, guava, muri, chira, doi and rice are all affordable and good for you. Seasonal fruit and vegetables are cheaper and fresher than out-of-season ones. Second, help your family plan. Once a week, spend 10 minutes thinking of the week's tiffins and snacks, so the shopping list includes them.

Third, prepare ahead. Boil a few eggs at once to keep in the fridge for two to three days. Keep a jar of roasted chola or peanuts for snacks. Pack your tiffin the night before: roti with vegetables, khichuri, or chira with doi and banana. Carry your own water bottle so you are not buying drinks. Fourth, when you do eat outside, choose better options: a fruit seller's guava or banana, jhalmuri with chola, or a plain roti and dal instead of fried singara every day.

Sabbir got 50 taka every day for tiffin and spent it on chips and a soft drink. By 1 pm, he was hungry again and grumpy. He and his mother made a plan: on Friday night, they boiled eggs and roasted chola for the week. Every morning, he packed a roti roll with egg and a banana. He still had chips once a week as a treat. At the end of the month, he had saved almost 1,000 taka, and he felt full and focused until school ended.

The common mistake is thinking healthy food must be expensive, like imported fruits, special oats or "diet" products. Simple home food like dal, eggs, vegetables and local fruit is among the healthiest and cheapest in the world.

Remember: pick cheap healthy heroes, plan once a week, prepare ahead, and pack your tiffin the night before.
key_points: Dal, eggs, chola, seasonal vegetables and local fruit are cheap and healthy.
Spend 10 minutes once a week planning tiffins and snacks.
Prepare ahead, like boiling eggs and roasting chola, and pack tiffin the night before.
Healthy food does not have to be expensive or imported.
lessons.tip: Boil a few eggs at once and keep them in the fridge for two or three days of quick tiffins.
lessons.task: Write down your tiffin or snack plan for the next three school days using only cheap foods from this lesson. Show it to whoever does the shopping at home.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cheap healthy food from the lesson?
quiz.explain: Chola, dal, eggs, seasonal vegetables and local fruit are affordable and healthy.

quiz.q: What is a smart way to save time on busy mornings?
options: Buy fried snacks on the way
Pack your tiffin the night before
quiz.explain: Packing tiffin the night before means you have a healthy meal ready even on rushed mornings.

quiz.q: What happened when Sabbir started packing tiffin from home?
options: He saved almost 1,000 taka a month and stayed full
quiz.explain: Home-packed roti, egg and banana kept him full, and he saved almost 1,000 taka in a month.

lessons.title: Stay active in any season
lessons.content:
Staying active in any season means having a plan for the hot months, the rainy months, the cold months and exam time, so your movement does not stop every time life changes. Think of it like having an umbrella in your bag. You do not stop going to school when it rains; you just bring the umbrella. Your exercise needs an "umbrella" too.

Why plan for seasons? Most people do not quit exercise on purpose. They stop because of one very hot week, a month of rain or exam pressure, and then never start again. Starting from zero is much harder than keeping a small habit going. If you keep even a little movement during hard seasons, you hold on to most of your fitness and it is easy to build up again later.

Here's the plan for each season. Hot summer: move in the cooler parts of the day, early morning or after sunset. Drink water before, during and after, wear light, loose clothes and rest in the shade if you feel too hot. Stop and cool down if you feel dizzy, sick or get a headache, because those can be signs of heat stress. Rainy season: have an indoor backup, like 15 minutes of skipping, dancing to songs, climbing the stairs of your building, or a bodyweight circuit of squats, push-ups and planks in your room.

Winter: it is great weather for outdoor games like badminton and cricket, so use it. Warm up a little longer, since cold muscles are stiffer. Exam season: do not cut movement completely. Shrink it. Even 10 to 15 minutes a day, like a short walk or a few stretches between study sessions, helps you focus better and sleep better. During Ramadan, if you fast, choose lighter activity, like an easy walk, and do it close to iftar or after iftar when you can drink water.

Tania played badminton every winter evening, but every summer and monsoon she stopped completely. By the next winter, she was out of breath after one game. This year, she made a season plan. In summer, she walked with her father at 6 am. In the rainy season, she did 15 minutes of skipping and squats on the veranda. During exams, she did a 10-minute walk after every two hours of study. When winter came, she was fitter than ever and won her first neighbourhood tournament match.

The common mistake is thinking "if I can't do my full workout, there's no point". A small version always beats nothing. Ten minutes keeps the habit alive.

Remember: in every season, change the time, place or size of your exercise, but never let it drop to zero.
key_points: Hard seasons stop most habits, so plan for heat, rain, cold and exams.
In summer, move early morning or after sunset and drink plenty of water.
In rain, use an indoor backup like skipping, stairs or a bodyweight circuit.
In busy times, shrink your workout to 10 to 15 minutes instead of stopping.
lessons.tip: Write down a 15-minute indoor workout now, like skipping, squats, push-ups and plank, so it is ready on the next rainy day.
lessons.task: Make a mini season plan: write one line each for summer, rainy season, winter and exam time, saying when and how you will move.

quiz.q: When is the best time to exercise outside in hot summer?
options: Never, stop for the whole summer
quiz.explain: Early morning and after sunset are cooler, which makes outdoor exercise safer in summer.

quiz.q: What should you do with exercise during exam season?
options: Shrink it to around 10 to 15 minutes a day
quiz.explain: Keeping a short 10 to 15 minute version keeps the habit alive and helps focus and sleep.

quiz.q: What did Tania do differently this year?
options: She only exercised in winter again
She made a plan for every season
She did a 3-hour workout on rainy days
quiz.explain: Tania planned walks in summer, indoor skipping in the rains and short walks in exams, so she stayed fit for winter.

lessons.title: Myths, fads and trustworthy advice
lessons.content:
A health myth is something many people believe about health that is not actually true. A fad is a trendy diet or trick that becomes popular fast and fades just as fast. Think of them like rumours at school. Everyone repeats them, they sound convincing, but when you check, they are wrong.

Why does this matter? Following wrong advice can waste your money, waste your time and sometimes harm your body. Some people skip meals, buy expensive pills or try extreme diets they saw on Facebook or YouTube, and end up feeling weak, sick or disappointed. Knowing how to spot bad advice protects you and your family.

Here are three common myths. Myth 1: "Doing sit-ups burns belly fat." Your body does not lose fat only from the part you exercise. Fat goes down slowly all over the body with regular activity, good food and sleep. Myth 2: "Skipping meals is the best way to get healthy." For growing kids especially, skipping meals leaves you tired, unfocused and very hungry later, so you often overeat junk. Myth 3: "Sweating a lot means you burned a lot of fat." Sweat is mostly water that cools you down. You sweat more in hot weather even when you do little.

Here's how to check any advice, using four questions. One: who is saying it? A doctor, nutritionist or trusted health organisation is more reliable than a random influencer. Two: are they selling something? If the post ends with "buy my product", be careful. Three: does it promise fast, magical results, like "lose 10 kg in a week" or "grow taller in 7 days"? Real changes take time, so big promises are a red flag. Four: does it tell you to cut out a whole food group or stop medicine? That needs a real doctor's advice, not an online post. When in doubt, ask a parent, teacher or doctor.

Nusrat's aunt shared a Facebook video saying "Drink this special tea for 7 days and lose all belly fat". It cost 1,500 taka a packet. Nusrat used the four questions: the person was not a doctor, they were selling the tea, and they promised magic results in 7 days. Three red flags! She showed her aunt the questions. Her aunt did not buy it and instead joined Nusrat's evening walks.

The common mistake is believing advice just because many people share it or because a famous person says it. Popular does not mean true. Check who says it, why and whether it sounds too good to be true.

Remember: be suspicious of quick magic, sellers and extreme rules, and trust real experts and slow, steady habits.
key_points: Sit-ups do not burn fat from your belly only; fat drops slowly all over the body.
Skipping meals usually leaves you tired and leads to overeating later.
Check advice: who says it, are they selling something, does it promise magic?
When unsure, ask a parent, teacher or doctor, not a random video.
lessons.tip: Before believing a health post, ask: who said it, are they selling something, and does it promise fast magic? Two yes answers is a big warning.
lessons.task: Find one health claim you have heard recently, on Facebook, YouTube or from someone. Run it through the four questions and write down how many red flags it has.

quiz.q: Does doing sit-ups burn fat from your belly only?
options: Yes, fat is lost only where you exercise
No, fat is lost slowly all over the body
Only if you sweat a lot
quiz.explain: Your body loses fat all over, slowly, through regular activity, good food and sleep, not just from the muscle you work.

quiz.q: Which of these is a red flag in health advice?
options: It promises to make you lose 10 kg in a week
quiz.explain: Big, fast, magical promises are a warning sign. Real changes take time.

quiz.q: Which red flags did Nusrat find in the tea video?
options: The person was not a doctor, was selling the tea and promised fast magic results
It was from a trusted health organisation
It was free and gave balanced advice
quiz.explain: The seller was not an expert, was selling the product and promised magic results in 7 days, three red flags.

lessons.title: Your long-term health plan
lessons.content:
A long-term health plan is a short list of simple habits you keep for years, not just for a few weeks. Think of it like brushing your teeth. You do not brush hard for one week and then stop. You do a little every day, and that is why your teeth last. Health works the same way: small daily habits beat big short bursts.

Why have one? Starting is easy, but most people slip back into old habits after a month or two. A clear plan helps you remember what matters most and gets you back on track when you slip. It also connects all the things you learned: moving, eating well, drinking water, sitting better, sleeping and checking advice. Over years, these habits help you grow strong, stay energetic, focus better in school and lower the risk of illnesses later in life.

Here's how to build your plan, using five pillars. Move: about 60 minutes a day, with strength 2 or 3 days a week. Eat: the balanced plate at most meals, a protein at every meal, fewer sugary drinks. Drink: about 6 to 8 glasses of water, more in heat. Sleep: kids around 6 to 12 years need about 9 to 12 hours, and teens about 8 to 10. Put screens away 30 to 60 minutes before bed, because the light and content keep your brain awake. Check: see a doctor for regular check-ups when your family arranges them, visit a dentist, and tell an adult if something in your body feels wrong instead of hiding it.

Now make it yours. Pick just one habit from each pillar that you will keep, and write the five lines on one page. For example: "Walk to tuition. Egg or dal at breakfast. Finish my water bottle at school. Phone away by 10 pm. Tell Ammu if I feel unwell." Stick it where you see it daily. Every month, look at it, tick what is working, and fix one thing that is not. If you miss a few days, do not start over from zero; just do the next small step today.

Rafi finished this course and made his five-line plan. In the first month, he kept four out of five, but the phone-away-by-10 rule kept failing. Instead of giving up, he changed it: he started charging his phone in the living room at night. That fixed it. Six months later, he was sleeping better, his cricket stamina was the best in his team, and his mother had copied his plan for herself.

The common mistake is trying to be perfect and quitting after a slip. Everyone misses days. What matters is coming back quickly, ideally the very next day.

Remember: five pillars, one habit each, written on one page, checked monthly, and restarted the day after any slip.
key_points: Long-term health comes from small daily habits kept for years.
Five pillars: move, eat, drink, sleep and check.
Kids need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep; teens about 8 to 10.
Missing a day is normal; restart with the next small step the very next day.
lessons.tip: Charge your phone outside your bedroom at night. It is the easiest way to protect your sleep.
lessons.task: Write your five-line health plan now: one habit each for move, eat, drink, sleep and check. Stick it somewhere you will see it every day.

quiz.q: What are the five pillars in the lesson?
options: Run, lift, swim, cycle and jump
Move, eat, drink, sleep and check
Diet, pills, gym, scale and apps
Study, play, eat, watch and sleep
quiz.explain: The five pillars are move, eat, drink, sleep and check, with one habit chosen from each.

quiz.q: About how much sleep do kids aged 6 to 12 need?
quiz.explain: Children aged about 6 to 12 need roughly 9 to 12 hours of sleep, and teens about 8 to 10.

quiz.q: What did Rafi do when his phone rule kept failing?
options: He gave up on the whole plan
He changed it to charging his phone in the living room
quiz.explain: Rafi adjusted the habit instead of quitting, and charging his phone outside his room fixed his sleep.
